Its embedding has three faces: the triangle A, B, C (tinted in the accent color), the triangle A, C, D (tinted teal), and the outer face, the region around the whole drawing, bounded by A, D, C, B (the dashed violet outline). The card lists each face as the cycle of nodes around it." width="100%"} A crossing-free drawing of a planar graph cuts the plane into regions, its *faces*, one of them the unbounded outer face. Each face is described by the walk of nodes around its boundary. For a connected graph there are `e - n + 2` of them (Euler's formula), and every edge borders two faces or, for a bridge, the same face twice, so the walks have `2e` steps in all. Faces are what planar duals, mesh processing, map coloring and face-based planar algorithms work with. The faces come from the embedding `check_planarity()` returns, traced as NetworkX's `PlanarEmbedding.faces()` traces them: start from a node and an edge leaving it, and at each node turn to the next edge in the clockwise order around it. A graph usually has several planar embeddings with different faces (only 3-connected planar graphs have just one), and the one here need not match NetworkX's. Edge direction, self-loops and parallel edges are ignored. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [list[list[int]]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : One list of node IDs per face, in order around it (the last node is joined back to the first). Walks repeat a node that the face's boundary passes more than once, as around a bridge or a cut node: a path `A - B` has the single face `[A, B]`, walked along both sides of its edge. Isolated nodes lie on no face, and each connected component with edges contributes its own outer face. ::: ## Raises {.doc-raises} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [ValueError]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If the graph is not planar. ::: ## See Also {.doc-see-also} [](`~check_planarity`) : The embedding the faces are traced from. ## Technical Notes {.doc-technical-notes} Every half-edge (an edge taken in one direction) lies on exactly one face, so tracing the face of each not yet visited half-edge, with nodes visited in ID order and their neighbors in clockwise order, finds every face once in `O(n + e)` time after the planarity test. ## Examples {.doc-examples} A square with one diagonal has three faces: the two triangles and the outer square: ::: {#b48c13a1 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec g = ec.Graph().add_nodes(["A", "B", "C", "D"]) g.add_edges([("A", "B"), ("B", "C"), ("C", "D"), ("D", "A"), ("A", "C")]) [[g.get_label_from_id(n) for n in face] for face in g.planar_faces()] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` [['A', 'B', 'C'], ['A', 'C', 'D'], ['A', 'D', 'C', 'B']] ``` ::: ::: A cube has six faces, each a square, as Euler's formula requires for 8 nodes and 12 edges: ::: {#66a35e35 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} cube = ec.Graph().add_hypercube_graph(3) faces = cube.planar_faces() len(faces), [len(f) for f in faces] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` (6, [4, 4, 4, 4, 4, 4]) ``` ::: :::
